body:
Why constitutional reforms became necessary

After the Revolt of 1857, the British Crown assumed direct control of India in 1858. Although the British government established legislative councils, Indians had little effective control over administration. Important decisions remained with the Viceroy, provincial Governors and British officials.

The Indian National Congress, established in 1885, initially demanded greater Indian representation in legislative councils, wider opportunities in public services and increased control over public expenditure. As the national movement developed, these demands expanded from participation in colonial institutions to responsible government and eventually independence.

Between 1909 and 1947, constitutional developments addressed different questions: Who could elect representatives? What powers would those representatives possess? Would ministers answer to elected legislatures? How would authority be divided between the Centre and provinces? Who would frame India's Constitution? Finally, when would British rule end?

Five concepts that must be distinguished

Representation

Representation means that members of a community or constituency participate in a legislative body through elected or nominated representatives. Increasing the number of Indian members did not necessarily make the government responsible to them.

Responsible government

In a system of responsible government, ministers must retain the confidence of the elected legislature to remain in office. Under early colonial reforms, an elected member might question government decisions without having the power to remove the executive.

Dyarchy

Dyarchy means dividing executive responsibility between 2 authorities. Under the Government of India Act, 1919, provincial subjects were divided between those administered by the Governor and his executive councillors and those administered by Indian ministers responsible to the provincial legislature.

Provincial autonomy

Provincial autonomy gives provincial governments authority over specified subjects through their own institutions. The Government of India Act, 1935, introduced a more responsible provincial system, although Governors retained important discretionary powers.

Constitution-making and transfer of power

A Constituent Assembly is a body formed to prepare or adopt a constitution. The Cabinet Mission Plan of 1946 proposed such an Assembly. The Indian Independence Act, 1947, subsequently provided the legal basis for ending British rule and establishing 2 independent Dominions.

Representation is not the same as responsible government. Likewise, a proposal to establish a political institution must be distinguished from an institution that actually began functioning. This distinction is especially important for the federal provisions of the Government of India Act, 1935.

The overall sequence

The reforms of 1909 expanded legislative representation. The Act of 1919 introduced limited provincial responsibility through dyarchy. The Act of 1935 replaced provincial dyarchy with provincial autonomy and proposed a federation that never came into operation. The Cripps proposals of 1942 discussed India's post-war constitutional future. The Cabinet Mission of 1946 proposed a united constitutional framework and a constitution-making body. The Indian Independence Act of 1947 transferred power to 2 Dominions.

Prelims focus

  • 1909: Indian Councils Act and Morley–Minto Reforms.
  • 1919: Government of India Act and provincial dyarchy.
  • 1935: Government of India Act and provincial autonomy.
  • 1946: Cabinet Mission Plan and Constituent Assembly arrangements.
  • 1947: Indian Independence Act and transfer of power.
  • Trap: An expanded legislature does not automatically mean an executive responsible to that legislature.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, Chapter 9, The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947, printed pp. 110–115 and 122–126; NCERT, Indian Constitution at Work, Class 11, Chapter 1, Constitution: Why and How?, pp. 2–5 and 15–16; Government of India Act, 1935, Parts II and III; Indian Independence Act, 1947, section 1. Online legislation consulted 22 November 2026.]

title: Constitutional Developments in British India: Background and Key Concepts

body:
The Indian Councils Act, 1909

The reforms commonly called the Morley–Minto Reforms were enacted through the Indian Councils Act, 1909. They were associated with John Morley, the Secretary of State for India in Britain, and Lord Minto, the Viceroy of India.

The reforms came at a time of growing political pressure. The Swadeshi movement had developed after the partition of Bengal in 1905, and Indian political organisations demanded a greater role in administration. The All-India Muslim League, established at Dacca in 1906, also demanded political safeguards, including separate Muslim representation.

Expansion of legislative councils

The Act increased the maximum number of additional members of the Central Legislative Council from 16 to 60 and expanded provincial legislative councils. It extended the elective principle, but elections remained indirect and restricted to small electorates.

Representatives could be returned through bodies or constituencies associated with municipalities, district boards, universities, chambers of commerce, landholders and other designated interests. Consequently, the system did not establish universal adult franchise.

Official and non-official majorities

An official member was a government official serving in the council. A non-official member was not serving as such a government official; the category could include both elected and nominated persons.

  • Central Legislative Council: The British government retained an official majority.
  • Provincial legislative councils: Non-official members formed a majority, but this did not mean that elected members controlled the provincial executive.

Non-official majority does not mean elected majority. A nominated non-official member was still a non-official member. The presence of more non-official members therefore did not establish responsible government.

Introduction of separate electorates

The most consequential electoral provision was the formal introduction of separate electorates for Muslims. Seats were allotted for Muslim representation, and eligible Muslim voters elected Muslim representatives for those seats.

A separate electorate should not be confused with a reserved seat under a joint electorate. In a joint electorate, eligible voters of different communities vote within the same constituency, even if the seat is reserved for a particular category of candidate. Under the separate Muslim electorates introduced in 1909, the electorate itself was defined by religious community.

This system institutionalised communal representation within the colonial electoral structure. It did not grant all Muslims the right to vote: voting qualifications remained restrictive.

Limited legislative powers

Legislative council members gained greater opportunities to discuss budgets, ask questions, including permitted supplementary questions, and move resolutions on matters of public interest. These powers provided a forum for criticism and discussion, but councils could not compel the executive to resign or establish full parliamentary control over the administration.

The reforms also coincided with the appointment of Satyendra Prasanno Sinha in 1909 as the first Indian member of the Viceroy's Executive Council. This was an appointment to the executive, not evidence that the executive had become responsible to an elected legislature.

Importance and limitations

The Act recognised a larger Indian presence in legislative institutions while preserving decisive British executive authority. It expanded political participation for a restricted electorate and introduced communal electoral arrangements. It therefore represented limited constitutional reform, not self-government or independence.

Prelims focus

  • Official name: Indian Councils Act, 1909.
  • Associated persons: John Morley and Lord Minto.
  • Central Legislative Council: Maximum number of additional members increased from 16 to 60.
  • Majority distinction: Official majority at the Centre; non-official majority in provincial councils.
  • Electoral innovation: Separate electorates for Muslims.
  • First Indian in the Viceroy's Executive Council: Satyendra Prasanno Sinha, 1909.
  • Trap: The reforms did not introduce responsible government or universal adult franchise.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, Chapter 9, printed p. 114; President's Secretariat, History of Parliamentary Democracy in India, Press Information Bureau, paragraphs 26–31, published 15 May 2017, consulted 22 November 2026; Indian Councils Act, 1909, provisions on legislative councils and elections.]

title: Morley–Minto Reforms, 1909: Legislative Expansion and Separate Electorates

body:
From the Montagu Declaration to the 1919 Act

During the First World War, Indian political leaders pressed for a definite advance towards self-government. On 20 August 1917, Edwin Montagu, the Secretary of State for India, announced the British government's objective of progressively developing responsible government in India while India remained within the British Empire.

Montagu and the Viceroy, Lord Chelmsford, developed reform proposals that became the basis of the Government of India Act, 1919. The Act received royal assent on 23 December 1919, and the new provincial arrangements operated from 1921.

The declaration was a statement of intended gradual development. It did not announce immediate independence or specify a definite date for transferring full power.

Dyarchy in the provinces

Provincial dyarchy was a system under which provincial administration was divided into reserved subjects, controlled by the Governor and executive councillors, and transferred subjects, administered by ministers responsible to the provincial legislature.

The Governor presided over both parts of the administration. The distinction lay in who exercised administrative responsibility for the subjects concerned.

FeatureReserved subjectsTransferred subjects
Principal authorityGovernor and executive councillorsMinisters appointed by the Governor; each had to be or become an elected member of the provincial legislature within 6 months
Typical subjectsPolice, administration of justice, land revenue and important financial mattersEducation, public health, agriculture and local self-government
ResponsibilityNot responsible to the elected provincial legislatureMinisters answerable to the provincial legislature
Governor's positionRetained direct executive authorityRetained significant supervisory and overriding powers

For example, a provincial minister could administer education, but major financial decisions remained influenced by authorities responsible for reserved subjects. The division frequently restricted the ability of Indian ministers to carry out their programmes.

Changes in the Central Legislature

The Act introduced a bicameral Central Legislature, consisting of the Council of State and the Legislative Assembly. Bicameral means that the legislature has 2 houses.

The legislature gained a wider representative element and increased opportunities for debate. Nevertheless, the Governor-General and his executive remained under British control. The central executive was not made responsible to the elected legislature.

Dyarchy was introduced in the provinces, not at the Centre, under the 1919 Act. The existence of a bicameral central legislature did not create central dyarchy.

Elections and communal representation

Provincial legislatures were enlarged, with elected members forming a substantial majority. However, voting rights depended on qualifications such as property, tax payment and other prescribed conditions. Most Indian adults remained outside the electorate.

The reforms retained separate electorates and extended communal or special electoral representation to additional groups, including Sikhs and certain other recognised communities and interests.

Why the reforms remained limited

Indian ministers gained experience in administering transferred subjects, but the most powerful offices remained beyond legislative control. The Governor could withhold assent from legislation, return bills for reconsideration or reserve bills for the consideration of the Governor-General.

The Act provided for a later review of the constitutional system. The British government appointed the Simon Commission in 1927 to examine the operation of the reforms, before the expected 10-year review period had fully elapsed.

Prelims focus

  • Montagu Declaration: 20 August 1917.
  • Government of India Act: 1919.
  • Provincial innovation: Dyarchy, dividing reserved and transferred subjects.
  • Central innovation: Bicameral legislature with the Council of State and Legislative Assembly.
  • Transferred examples: Education, public health, agriculture and local self-government.
  • Trap: The 1919 Act did not introduce dyarchy at the Centre or full responsible government.

[House of Lords Library, Lord Sinha of Raipur and the Government of India Act 1919, research briefing, 13 December 2019, sections on the Montagu Declaration and main provisions of the Act, consulted 22 November 2026; Government of India Act, 1919, provisions on provincial administration and legislative councils; Supreme Court of India, judgment dated 8 April 2025, discussion of the Government of India Act, 1919, paragraph 52.]

title: Montagu–Chelmsford Reforms, 1919: Provincial Dyarchy and Limited Responsibility

body:
The Simon Commission, 1927

The British government appointed the Indian Statutory Commission, commonly called the Simon Commission, in 1927 to review the constitutional arrangements established by the Government of India Act, 1919.

It was chaired by Sir John Simon and consisted entirely of British members. The absence of Indian members provoked strong opposition. When the Commission arrived in India in 1928, it faced widespread protests and boycotts.

The Commission considered constitutional changes, including the future of provincial administration. Its recommendations contributed to subsequent British discussions of constitutional reform, but the Commission itself did not enact the Government of India Act, 1935.

The Nehru Report, 1928

Indian leaders attempted to formulate their own constitutional proposals. A committee chaired by Motilal Nehru prepared the Nehru Report in 1928.

The report recommended Dominion status, a parliamentary system and constitutional arrangements based on joint electorates, with specified safeguards for minorities. Dominion status meant substantial self-government while retaining a constitutional association with the British Crown. It was not the same as an independent republic.

Disagreement continued over minority representation and the division of authority between the Centre and provinces. In 1929, Muhammad Ali Jinnah presented his Fourteen Points, emphasising minority safeguards, provincial autonomy and separate electorates.

Demand for complete independence

At its Lahore Session in December 1929, the Indian National Congress adopted Purna Swaraj, or complete independence, as its objective. This was a major change from constitutional proposals seeking Dominion status within the British imperial framework.

The difference matters: Dominion status proposed substantial self-government with a continuing constitutional connection to the Crown; Purna Swaraj demanded complete independence.

Three Round Table Conferences

The British government convened 3 Round Table Conferences in London to discuss India's constitutional future. They took place in 1930, 1931 and 1932.

ConferenceYearKey fact
First1930The Congress did not participate.
Second1931Mahatma Gandhi attended as the Congress representative.
Third1932The Congress did not participate.

Gandhi attended the Second Round Table Conference following the Gandhi–Irwin Pact of 5 March 1931. The conferences discussed federation, provincial responsibility and minority representation, but they did not produce an agreement acceptable to all major political interests.

Communal Award and Poona Pact, 1932

In 1932, British Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald announced the Communal Award, which included separate electoral arrangements for the Depressed Classes.

After negotiations involving Mahatma Gandhi, B. R. Ambedkar and other representatives, the Poona Pact of 24 September 1932 provided for reserved seats for the Depressed Classes within joint electorates instead of separate electorates for them.

This provides an important contrast with the Muslim separate electorates introduced in 1909. A reserved seat and a separate electorate are different mechanisms of representation.

Connection with the Government of India Act, 1935

The Simon Commission's work, Indian constitutional proposals, Round Table Conference discussions and subsequent British deliberations shaped the preparation of the Government of India Act, 1935. They also demonstrated that a constitutional settlement depended not only on the division of governmental powers but on agreement over representation.

Prelims focus

  • Simon Commission: Appointed in 1927; chaired by Sir John Simon; no Indian members.
  • Nehru Report: 1928; chaired by Motilal Nehru; recommended Dominion status.
  • Jinnah's Fourteen Points: 1929.
  • Congress Purna Swaraj resolution: Lahore Session, December 1929.
  • Round Table Conferences: 1930, 1931 and 1932; Gandhi attended only the Second.
  • Poona Pact: 24 September 1932.
  • Trap: The Nehru Report of 1928 and the Purna Swaraj resolution of 1929 did not demand the same constitutional status.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, Chapter 9, printed pp. 120–122; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part III, Class 12, Chapter 13, Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement, section on the Round Table Conference; Motilal Nehru Committee, Nehru Report, 1928, constitutional recommendations; Government of India Act, 1935, historical background; House of Commons and House of Lords parliamentary records concerning constitutional reform in India, consulted 22 November 2026.]
